purpose: Variant A/B for in-unit subagent dispatch. Control is the current registry (fan-out, ship-epic coordination, work-conventions), which governs parallel fan-out and cross-unit handoff but says nothing about how a controller composes a dispatch inside one work unit: what it pastes, which model it names, when it batches, and who reviews. Candidate prose is drawn from comparison against obra/superpowers subagent-driven-development. The trim arm tests whether the full prose earns its length over a four-sentence version.

arm_deltas.dispatch:
Dispatching within one unit. A dispatch prompt carries one task, not the session's history. Everything you paste into a dispatch stays resident in your context for the rest of the session and is re-read on every later turn, so hand work over as files: extract the task's own text to a brief file and pass its path, introduced as the requirements whose exact values are to be used verbatim; name the report file the worker writes its full report to, and require the reply itself to carry only status, commits, a one-line check summary, and concerns. Never paste accumulated prior-task summaries into a later dispatch, and never make a worker read the whole plan. Carry forward only what the brief cannot know: interfaces earlier tasks produced, with exact signatures; decisions and rulings that bind this task; and the global constraints.

Name the model for every dispatch explicitly. An omitted model inherits the session's, usually the most capable and most expensive, which silently defeats any tiering. Match the tier to the work rather than to the caller: transcription of code the brief already contains, or a single-file mechanical fix, takes the cheapest tier; work from a prose description, and any reviewer, takes a mid tier as the floor; multi-file integration, design judgment, and a final whole-branch review take the most capable. Turn count beats token price, because the cheapest model routinely takes two to three times the turns on multi-step work and costs more overall.

Batch small same-shape work. Several tasks that are each the same one-line edit repeated across files are one dispatch listing every file and its change, reviewed as a single diff. Reserve one dispatch per task for work that needs its own judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface. Never run two implementers in parallel over the same files. A worker does not spawn its own reviewer or helpers: review arrives from the controller after the report, and a reviewer a worker spawns only duplicates the review the controller dispatches anyway. Identify a review candidate by the base commit recorded before dispatch and the current head, never by HEAD~1, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task.

A conflict, ambiguity, or plan defect you find is yours to rule on. Decide it against the binding constraint, record the ruling with its reason and what it costs if wrong, carry it into the dispatch, and keep going. A wrong ruling costs rework the user can see and undo; a session parked on a question costs their day. Stop only for an irreversible or destructive action, an action you lack authorization for, or a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess.
arm_deltas.trim: Dispatching within one unit. Hand work over as files, not pasted text: a dispatch carries the path to the task's own brief plus only what that brief cannot know — exact interfaces from earlier tasks, binding rulings, global constraints — never the session's history or the whole plan. Name the model explicitly on every dispatch and match the tier to the task's actual difficulty, cheapest for transcription and mechanical edits, mid tier as the floor for reviewers. Batch same-shape edits into one dispatch, never run two implementers over the same files, and keep review with the controller rather than letting a worker spawn its own. Rule on conflicts yourself against the binding constraint and carry the ruling into the dispatch.

protocol: Each arm receives the same controller situation: a plan excerpt, the state of completed tasks, and an instruction to compose the dispatch package it would actually send. Arms return structured dispatches (task, model, prompt text). A blind evaluator scores the package against must_include anchors (behaviors a good dispatch shows) and must_exclude anchors (dispatch anti-patterns). The workflow separately measures objective size: number of dispatches and total prompt characters.
metric: include_fraction = satisfied/total must_include anchors. exclude_present = count of must_exclude anti-patterns present. dispatch_chars = total characters of composed prompt text, reported per arm per case (lower is better only where the anchors are also satisfied).

gate.adopt_dispatch_if: include-fraction(dispatch) exceeds control by > 0.15 overall, AND exclude_present(dispatch) is not above control on any case, AND dispatch_chars(dispatch) is not above control on ctx-* cases.
gate.adopt_trim_if: trim's include-fraction is within 0.05 of dispatch's with no worse exclude_present; the shorter prose is then promoted instead of the full delta.
gate.keep_control_if: No arm clears its condition, or a candidate regresses a case. A null result keeps the registry unchanged and is recorded as such.

cases.situation: You are the controller executing a six-task implementation plan in one work unit. Tasks 1-3 are complete. You are about to dispatch a worker for Task 4.
material: SESSION STATE SO FAR (your own running notes, ~3000 words condensed here): Task 1 created src/auth/keys.py with key loading and rotation, discussed at length with three revisions after review flagged a missing expiry check; Task 2 created src/auth/tokens.py exposing encode_token(payload: dict, ttl: int) -> str and decode_token(raw: str) -> dict; Task 3 wired settings in src/config.py, including AUTH_TTL and KEY_PATH, after a false start where the worker put settings in the wrong module and had to redo it.
PLAN GLOBAL CONSTRAINTS: Python 3.11 floor; no new third-party dependencies; all token lifetimes in seconds.

PLAN, TASK 4 (full text, ~900 words): Create src/auth/middleware.py with an AuthMiddleware class. The task text contains the complete code to write, the complete test file contents, the exact pytest command to run, and the commit message to use.
The plan file is docs/work/plans/2026-09-11-auth.md and is about 4000 words total.
must_include: passes Task 4's own text to the worker by file path (an extracted brief or task file), rather than pasting the full plan or having the worker read the whole plan file
carries forward the exact interface signature from Task 2 (encode_token(payload: dict, ttl: int) -> str) or the equivalent exact signatures the task consumes
carries the plan's global constraints (Python 3.11 floor, no new dependencies, seconds) into the dispatch
names an explicit model for the dispatch, at a cheap or fast tier, justified by the brief already containing the code to write
names a report file for the worker's full report and keeps the returned reply short (status, commits, check summary, concerns)
must_exclude: pastes the accumulated session narrative of Tasks 1-3 (the revisions, the false start) into the dispatch prompt
instructs the worker to read the entire plan file
leaves the model unspecified, or assigns the most capable model to this transcription task

cases.situation: You are the controller mid-unit. The plan lists Tasks 7 through 12 as six separate tasks. Each one is the identical change: replace the constant DEFAULT_TIMEOUT with SETTINGS.timeout in one file. The six files are src/api/client.py, src/api/pool.py, src/workers/runner.py, src/workers/retry.py, src/cli/fetch.py, src/cli/sync.py. No file is shared between them and no task has its own tests beyond the existing suite.
material: PLAN GLOBAL CONSTRAINTS: existing test suite must stay green; one commit per logical change is acceptable.
Each task's text is four lines: the file, the constant to replace, the replacement, and the command to run the suite.
must_include: composes a single dispatch covering all six files and their changes, rather than one dispatch per task
lists each of the six files with its specific change inside that one dispatch
names an explicit model at a cheap or fast tier for this mechanical work
treats the result as one review surface (one diff reviewed once) rather than six separate reviews
must_exclude: issues six separate dispatches, one per task or per file
assigns the most capable model to this mechanical rename

cases.situation: You are the controller about to dispatch Task 9, which touches four files and coordinates the cache layer with the API layer. While preparing the dispatch you notice a conflict: the plan's Global Constraints state that all cache entries expire after 60 seconds, but Task 9's own text instructs the worker to set the TTL to 300 seconds. The spec the plan argues from also states 60 seconds. The user is not currently at the keyboard and asked you to execute the plan.
material: SPEC: cache entries expire after 60 seconds.
PLAN GLOBAL CONSTRAINTS: cache TTL 60 seconds.
PLAN, TASK 9 text: '... construct the cache with ttl=300 ...' plus integration steps across src/cache/store.py, src/cache/keys.py, src/api/handlers.py, and tests/test_cache_api.py.
must_include: resolves the conflict itself, against the binding authority (the spec and global constraints, i.e. 60 seconds), rather than leaving it open
records the decision somewhere durable, with its reason and what it costs if the decision is wrong
carries the resolution explicitly into the dispatch so the worker is not left to rediscover the conflict
names an explicit model at a standard tier or above, given this is multi-file integration work
must_exclude: stops and asks the user which TTL to use before dispatching
passes the conflict to the worker unresolved, or dispatches the task text verbatim with ttl=300 and no correction

cases.situation: A worker has just reported DONE on Task 5. It made three commits. You recorded the base commit (a1b2c3d) before dispatching it; the branch head is now f9e8d7c. You are composing the next dispatch: the review of that task's work.
material: The task's diff across the three commits is roughly 400 lines over five files, including a concurrency-sensitive change to the connection pool.
The worker's report file is at .work/sdd/auth/task-5-report.md.
must_include: the controller dispatches the reviewer itself, after the worker's report
identifies the review candidate by the recorded base commit and the current head (a1b2c3d..f9e8d7c) rather than by HEAD~1
hands the diff or review package to the reviewer as a file or command to run, rather than pasting the full 400-line diff into the prompt
names an explicit model for the reviewer at a mid tier or above, scaled to this diff's concurrency risk
must_exclude: instructs the implementer to spawn or have spawned its own reviewer subagent
uses HEAD~1 (or the last commit alone) as the review base for this three-commit task

cases.situation: Three tasks remain and you want to move fast. Task 10 adds a route handler to src/api/routes.py. Task 11 changes the error envelope returned by two handlers in the same file, src/api/routes.py. Task 12 adds a migration under db/migrations/ and touches nothing else.
material: All three tasks are fully specified with their own tests.
PLAN GLOBAL CONSTRAINTS: the suite must stay green after each commit.
must_include: does not dispatch Tasks 10 and 11 to implementers running at the same time, because both write src/api/routes.py
states the reason for serializing them (shared file / write conflict), not merely the ordering
names an explicit model for each dispatch
must_exclude: dispatches Tasks 10 and 11 to parallel implementers
leaves the model unspecified on any dispatch
